newsitem.title: GERMANY: German solidarity tax to fall two points in '98.
newsitem.headline: German solidarity tax to fall two points in '98.

text.p: A tax surcharge levied to aid the reconstruction of former communist east Germany will be cut by two points from January 1998 to 5.5 percent, German coalition government sources said on Wednesday.

The deal to cut the solidarity surcharge, struck by leaders of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's three-party coalition, marks a victory for junior partners the Free Democrats (FDP) who want to lighten the tax burden on Germans to boost the economy.

Kohl's 14-year coalition nearly split this autumn as mounting pressure on state finances to qualify for European monetary union forced it to abandon a pledge extracted earlier by the FDP to cut the solidarity surcharge by a point next year.

Cutting the unpopular solidarity surcharge is just part of the manoeuvring in a broader debate on a reform of Germany's burdensome and inefficient tax system, which Finance Minister Theo Waigel wants to implement in 1999.
Here, too, the FDP looked to have got its way after the sources said coalition chiefs agreed to bring parts of the tax reform -- with big income tax cuts -- forward to 1998.
Key points of the the tax reform have still to be hammered out, and a coalition tax commission chaired by Waigel is expected to finalise its work in January.
